stories.title: FDA clears AI that predicts 5-year breast cancer risk from mammograms
bullets: Works on images already taken, so no extra scan or questionnaire is needed; the output is a risk score, not a finding
Validated on 65,000+ screening mammograms from 10 US sites, with consistent performance reported in Black women and dense breasts; no accuracy numbers released
Not a cancer detector, no outcome data yet, and not the first: rival Clairity's tool for standard 2D mammograms won FDA De Novo authorization in May 2025
stories.why: Image-based risk could replace questionnaire models like Tyrer-Cuzick when deciding who needs supplemental MRI or shorter screening intervals.
stories.question: If AI flagged high 5-year risk on a normal mammogram, what would you do differently, and what evidence would you want first?

terms.def: The standard breast cancer risk calculator (also called IBIS), filled in from a questionnaire: age, family history, reproductive and hormonal history, and breast density. In the US, a lifetime risk of 20% or more usually qualifies a woman for annual screening MRI.
The two main FDA routes for devices. 510(k): 'substantially equivalent' to a device already on the market, needs less clinical evidence. De Novo: a genuinely new kind of device, needs more.

stories.dek: DeepHealth, the AI subsidiary of US outpatient-imaging chain RadNet, makes Mammo Risk: software that reads a woman's routine 3D mammogram and estimates her chance of developing breast cancer over the next 3–5 years.

stories.title: AI-designed drugs are genuinely outperforming in Phase II
bullets: Oliver Wyman analysis: AI-native drug developers progressed 45% of Phase II programs successfully, vs 29% for the broader sector (46-program sample)
AI drug discovery investment and licensing deals hit $46 billion in H1 2026 — after $43B in 2025 and just $12B in 2024
Money is following results: the data suggests AI-designed pipelines have measurable, trial-level signal — not just hype
stories.why: AI-native pharma pipelines are scaling fast — clinical teams will increasingly see AI-designed drugs in trials and eventually in practice.

terms.def: An ordinary medicine (pill or biologic) where machine-learning models helped choose the target or design the molecule. It passes the same trials and approval as any drug: 'AI' describes how it was found, not how it works.

stories.question: Would knowing a drug was AI-designed change how you read its trial data?
stories.dek: Consulting firm Oliver Wyman compared drug candidates from 'AI-native' biotechs, companies built around machine-learning drug design, with the rest of the industry and found more of them pass mid-stage trials.

stories.title: GPT-6.2 Astra ships to harsh reviews — but tops the med-chemistry benchmark
bullets: OpenAI released GPT-6.2 Astra and Sol on Nov 17; early reception was sharply negative — one prominent tester called it the 'worst model OpenAI has ever released'
Yet on MedChemBench (a 99-item medicinal-chemistry task set) Astra earned 84.5% — a leading score, though the benchmark itself cautions it does not prove real drug-discovery capability
Google answered Nov 18 with Gemini 4 Neon at $3/$15 per million tokens and a one-million-token context window — the price war continues
stories.why: Frontier labs now ship medical-science benchmarks alongside each release — a clear signal of where they think the value is heading.

terms.def: A token is ~¾ of a word; models are priced per million tokens. The context window is how much the model can read at once: 1M tokens ≈ 750,000 words, enough for many complete patient records.

stories.question: What would convince you an AI model is clinically competent: a benchmark score, or something else?
stories.dek: OpenAI, the maker of ChatGPT, released its newest model, GPT-6.2 Astra. Testers panned it for everyday use, but it topped MedChemBench, a test of medicinal-chemistry knowledge; Google's rival model Gemini launched the next day.

briefs.title: Anthropic's $2 trillion Nasdaq debut, the largest IPO on record
briefs.note: The maker of Claude, a model many clinical AI tools are built on, is now public and heavily capitalized. No direct patient impact.

briefs.title: FDA clears a2z-Omni-Triage: abdomen-pelvis CT triage flagging nine findings
briefs.note: A triage tool reorders the reading worklist so suspected urgent findings are read first. It doesn't make the diagnosis.

briefs.title: Chat 4 Heart trial: patients want health chatbots tailored to their own lives
briefs.note: Qualitative study within an NIH trial: ease of use and messages fitted to personal and cultural context mattered most.

signals.title: AI is now auditing the medical literature itself
signals.note: An MIT / Dana-Farber team used language models to review nearly 4,000 clinical prediction papers (Nature Medicine) and found that sharing code is still uncommon.
signals.later: AI-assisted peer review and reproducibility checks could change which studies we trust, and feeds into a new reporting guideline (TRIPOD-Code).

signals.title: Physicians report AI shaping their conversations with patients
signals.note: A Spherix survey of 396 U.S. physicians describes AI's growing influence on clinical decisions and on what patients bring into the consultation.
signals.later: Patients arriving with an AI 'second opinion' may become routine, and consultations will need a way to handle it.

glossary.def: Initial public offering: a private company sells shares on a stock exchange for the first time. It raises cash and requires public, audited reporting, so outsiders learn far more about how the company works and earns money.
The standard reporting checklist for studies of clinical prediction models, the equivalent of CONSORT for trials. TRIPOD-Code would add rules for sharing the analysis code.
